conventions.convention: Inputs have a finite independent product Borel probability law. Its restriction to the product of marginal supports has full mass and uses the trace Borel sigma-algebra; no completion is specified.

An admissible cutoff requires finite absolute moments through degree 2p_j and positive-definite monomial Gram matrices. Every chaos index lies in the cutoff box; these assumptions assert no polynomial completeness.
Gram–Schmidt uses the ordered monomials starting at degree zero, positive normalization, and consequently positive leading coefficients and constant mode 1.

The spatial space is real H0¹ on a bounded polyhedral open set, with the gradient norm. Parameter support is bounded, coefficient ellipticity holds for every supported parameter and almost every spatial point, and forcing is bounded affine.
Christoffel sampling requires a finite index set containing zero, uses density K/N and weights N/K, and returns coefficients only when the empirical Gram spectrum lies in [1/2,3/2].
Quadrature is applied to an evaluable representative at declared nodes; its finite weights need not be positive.

The finite-element rate assumes an exact finite chaos expansion, coefficient H^r regularity, bounded reference degrees of freedom, and a conforming boundary-preserving interpolant on shape-regular matching affine meshes.

load_bearing.statement: Throughout the pair, assume the selected cutoff vector is admissible. Admissibility requires the finite 2p_j absolute moment and positive-definite monomial Gram matrix in every coordinate; it does not assert polynomial density.

For indices in the admissible degree box, each tensor polynomial belongs to L²(ρ), and its integral pairing with another tensor is one when their indices agree and zero otherwise. When zero belongs to the index set, the family includes ψ₀=1.

Assume Countable Choice. For the defined L²ρ(V), the displayed integral pairing is a well-defined real inner product, its induced norm is complete, and finite-valued strongly measurable functions are dense.

For finite Λ containing zero and real u∈L²(ρ), the residual is orthogonal to the chaos space, the squared norm equals the sum of squared coefficients plus squared residual norm, E[u]=c₀, and variance equals the nonconstant coefficient sum plus squared residual norm.
For independent Christoffel samples and 0<δ<1, M≥12N log(2N/δ) implies that the empirical Gram spectrum lies in [1/2,3/2] with probability at least 1−δ.

Under Countable Choice and the affine diffusion hypotheses, a finite chaos index set inside the admissible cutoff box and a finite-dimensional conforming spatial subspace give a unique stochastic Galerkin solution whose Bochner error is at most a*/a_* times best approximation error.

concerns.concern: The definition takes all strongly measurable maps with square-integrable norm and defines their inner product by integrating the pointwise pairing, but the underlying probability space has the uncompleted trace Borel sigma-algebra. Strong measurability here permits arbitrary values on measurable null sets. For uniform ρ on [0,1], choose a Borel null Cantor set C and a non-Borel subset A⊂C. With V=R, U=2·1_A−1_C is strongly measurable (zero simple approximants converge outside C), and |U|²=1_C is Borel integrable. W=1 also qualifies, but UW=U is not Borel measurable. Thus the displayed inner-product integral is not defined under the stated scalar integration convention. This also affects the well-definedness assertion and Step 1.1 of thm-finite-input-bochner-l2-is-hilbert. A measurable-version integration convention is used later in proofs but is not fixed by this definition.

The Statement says the scalar form and load functions 'are measurable and integrable' for U,W in the defined Bochner space. Step 1.1 further says 'Defining the scalar function arbitrarily on the measurable exceptional null set gives a measurable representative.' Arbitrary modifications on null sets need not be measurable for the explicitly uncompleted Borel law. Concretely, take uniform parameter law on [0,1], cutoff zero, spatial D=(0,1), a=1, a nonzero v∈H0¹(D), a Borel null Cantor set C, and non-Borel A⊂C. Set U(y)=(2·1_A(y)−1_C(y))v and W(y)=v. Both satisfy strong measurability and have measurable square-integrable norms, but a_y(U(y),W(y))=(2·1_A−1_C)||v||² is not Borel measurable. Having a measurable version does not establish the Statement's literal measurability assertion.

seams_checked.note: The spatial-rate corollary preserves the supplier's dimension restriction, matching affine shape-regular meshes, bounded reference degrees of freedom, and ℓ≤r≤k+1. Global conformity and boundary preservation are explicit additional assumptions.

The stochastic Galerkin theorem applies the real Hilbert-space Céa result with Countable Choice, a finite-dimensional conforming subspace, and constants M=a* and α=a_*. No dual-regularity or Aubin–Nitsche conclusion is imported.

The Gaussian coefficient corollary assumes the supplier's Gaussian moment data and m_j≥p_j+1, checks coordinate product degrees ≤2p_j≤2m_j−1, and explicitly uses the product-moment-to-product-measure lemma. The work example correctly uses three cubature nodes per coordinate.

This is contextual rather than a direct item-level theorem invocation. The UQ page distinguishes its weighted least-squares procedure from spectral Galerkin and makes no universal equivalence or inherited spectral-rate claim.

The Smolyak coefficient corollary retains the uniform cube law, dyadic Simpson hierarchy, n≥2d, continuous mixed fourth derivatives with the supplier's endpoint convention, and dimension-dependent constants.

The affine model uses the proved separable real H0¹ Hilbert structure on bounded polyhedral open sets under Countable Choice. Its gradient norm is explicitly related to the supplier's Sobolev norm by norm equivalence.

The sensitivity page explicitly separates completeness from finite chaos orthogonality. Its complete-tensor Sobol theorem assumes completeness separately, and the two-state polynomial-chaos example verifies its finite Gram matrices, orthonormality, and completeness directly on four outcomes.
